title: Pale Ratifies the Dayton Framework
sources: General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina (Dayton), UN S/1995/999
content:
Slobodan Milošević initialled the General Framework Agreement at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base on 21 November 1995, under the joint-delegation authority the Pale leadership had granted on 30 August 1995. The text fixed Annex 1-A (the IFOR deployment, Zone of Separation, and heavy-weapons cantonment), Annex 2 (the 51:49 Inter-Entity Boundary Line), and Annex 4 (the Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution dividing the state into the Federation and the Republika Srpska).

For Pale the agreement was bittersweet. It recognized the RS as a constitutive entity — the territorial statehood the Bosnian Serb leadership had fought for since 1992 — but at 49 percent rather than the 70 percent the VRS had held at its peak, and inside a single Bosnian state rather than in union with Serbia. The Six Strategic Goals were, in their maximal form, abandoned. Milošević, not Karadžić, held the pen; the Pale leadership that had rejected every prior framework now faced ratifying one negotiated over its head.

The choice was between accepting the Dayton constitutional order — entity statehood at the cost of the maximal war aims — or holding a hardline rejectionist posture against a settlement that Belgrade, the great powers, and the post-Storm military balance had already made inevitable. Historically the RS accepted, through the Belgrade-led delegation, and the agreement was signed in Paris on 14 December 1995.

The posture recorded here is the last of the war's strategic choices: whether the Republika Srpska took its entity statehood inside Bosnia or refused the order that defined it.
